title: Why Data Persistence Matters 💡
description: Understand the ephemeral nature of containers and why you need volumes for stateful apps.

slides.title: Containers Are Born to Die 💀
slides.content:
# Ephemeral by Design

Docker containers are meant to be disposable. When you remove a container, its writable layer (all file changes) is gone forever.

- Database files, user uploads, logs – all vanish if stored inside the container.
- This is great for stateless apps, but most real‑world apps need **persistent data**.

Docker provides two main solutions:
1. **Volumes** – managed by Docker, stored outside the container’s filesystem.
2. **Bind mounts** – any directory on the host mounted into the container.

We’ll master both in this chapter.

slides.title: Why Not Just Keep Data Inside? 🤔

quizData.question: What happens to files created inside a container when the container is removed?

options.text: They are automatically saved to a volume
They are permanently lost (unless committed or stored in a volume)
They are moved to the host’s /tmp directory
They are backed up to Docker Hub

quizData.explanation: The container’s writable layer is removed along with the container. Only data stored in volumes or bind mounts survives.

slides.title: Volumes vs Bind Mounts – Quick Comparison ⚖️
slides.content:
# The Two Pillars

| Feature         | Volumes                  | Bind Mounts               |
|-----------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| Managed by      | Docker                   | Host filesystem           |
| Location        | `/var/lib/docker/volumes/` (default) | Any host path you choose |
| Portability     | Easier to share between containers | Tied to host directory structure |
| Use case        | Persistent app data (DB files, uploads) | Development (live code reloading, config files) |

> Think volumes as the “Docker way” – portable and decoupled from host layout.

slides.title: The Data Loss Demo 🎭
slides.codeSnippet:
# Create a container, write a file inside
docker run --name temp alpine touch /data.txt

# Stop and remove the container
docker rm temp

# Run another container from the same image – the file is gone!
docker run --rm alpine ls /data.txt   # error: No such file or directory

quizData.question: Committing a container with `docker commit` is the recommended way to persist data.
quizData.explanation: Committing creates an image from the container's state, but it's not meant for ongoing data persistence. Volumes separate data from the container lifecycle.

slides.title: Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Stateful = Volumes
For any container that must remember something (database, key‑value store, file storage), plan your volume strategy from the start.
